summary: Login slowness and 503s on auth-service are caused by CPU saturation at a provisioning ceiling: a ~3.8x request-rate surge (≈390 → ~1500 req/s) starting 06:50-06:53Z pinned auth-service CPU at ~97% with memory flat, saturated the worker pool (active=64/64, queues to 98763), and filled the server accept queue, so POST /v1/auth/login was rejected with 'accept queue full' 503s and p99 rose to ~3.8s; the autoscaler wanted 14 replicas but was capped at maxReplicas=8. This is H1 at confidence 0.60 (medium), and it is clearly ahead of the alternatives. The reporter's bcrypt-regression theory (H3) is decisively excluded — there was no auth-service deployment or functional config change in the window — and the shared redis-cache/portfolio-service path (H2) is now affirmatively contradicted by flat redis and neighbour telemetry. Confidence is capped by one unresolved hop: the origin of the surge (genuine external load vs retry amplification, H5 at 0.15) cannot be measured with the available telemetry.

ranked_hypotheses.title: Auth-service CPU saturation from a genuine load surge exceeding provisioned capacity (maxReplicas=8 cap)
ranked_hypotheses.statement: auth-service hit a CPU-bound capacity ceiling at ~06:50-06:55Z. Request rate rose ~3.8x (390 -> ~1500 req/s) driving cpu_pct ~38%->~97% with memory flat, saturating the worker pool (active=64/64, queue up to 98763) and the server accept queue, so POST /v1/auth/login was rejected 503 ('accept queue full') and p99 rose to ~3.8s. The autoscaler TRIED to compensate and could not: desired replicas 14 exceeded maxReplicas 8 (F29), and restarts stayed 0 with the process live at the ceiling (F28). The fault is that a load surge outgrew the provisioned replica cap; there is no faulty code/config on auth-service, and the shared redis-cache path is affirmatively healthy (F31-F33).

causal_chain.claim: A ~3.8x surge in request rate to auth-service begins at ~06:50-06:51Z (390 -> ~1500 req/s)
auth-service CPU saturates in lockstep (~38%->~97% pinned, memory flat, restarts 0) — a live process at a capacity ceiling, not a crash loop or GC event
The autoscaler attempts to add capacity but is capped: 'desired replicas 14 exceeds maxReplicas 8' — the load exceeds the provisioned ceiling, the defining capacity_saturation condition

CPU-bound worker-pool/accept-queue exhaustion produces the 503s and latency: pool pinned active=64/64, all ERROR logs are 'accept queue full, returning 503' on POST /v1/auth/login, error_rate 0.2%->14%, p99 -> ~3.8s

The gateway is blocked waiting on the saturated auth-service (its own p99 tracks ~3.8s), not the reverse; its ingress grew >= what it forwards, arguing against a single-caller retry storm against auth-service
No auth-service deployment or auth-relevant config change exists in the window; the only auth change is a non-functional log.level flip

No shared downstream component is degraded: redis-cache CPU/hit-ratio/connections are flat and healthy, no neighbour CPU deviates, portfolio-service (sole deployer) p99 is flat, and neither redis nor any service received a deploy/config change
The ultimate origin of the increased login load (which client/traffic source) is unidentified — no per-caller/per-endpoint dimension exists

assumptions: The request-rate increase is genuine exogenous/edge load rather than a retry storm whose retries originate only inside our telemetry
No autoscaling/limit change explains why maxReplicas is 8 (the cap itself is not a suspect change)
The ~3.8x surge does not originate in a shared upstream that also feeds the broader edge (no such component is identified, but per-caller breakdown is unavailable per F36)

ranked_hypotheses.title: Retry/amplification storm: client or gateway retries after early login failures drive the surge
ranked_hypotheses.statement: The ~3.8x request-rate rise could be a consequence rather than a cause: a moderate initial slowdown (or early failures) caused clients and/or api-gateway to retry failed/slow logins, multiplying request rate ~3.8x, which then saturated auth-service CPU and the accept queue. On this reading the surge is a feedback symptom and the origin is retry behaviour (or whatever caused the first failures) rather than provisioned capacity. The critic rightly notes this was dismissed on an indirect aggregate-rate argument; however the gateway-ingress evidence (F25/F38/F41) still tilts against a single-caller retry origin, and no retry counter can be measured (F37).

causal_chain.claim: Some initial trigger causes a small fraction of login requests to fail or slow
Clients/api-gateway retry the failed logins, multiplying request rate — note gateway retries cannot be measured: retries_per_min -> not_found, gateway emits no logs
Retries push auth-service CPU to ~97% and saturate the accept queue, with ~900 req/min rate-limited

Counter-evidence: gateway's OWN ingress request_rate rises ~3.9-4.1x in the identical 06:50-06:58 ramp, i.e. load is elevated at/above the gateway ingress, not only on gateway->auth retries — though clients could still be retrying through the edge

assumptions: The initial trigger could be any transient not itself observable in the findings
Client-side retry behaviour exists (common) but is not directly evidenced; gateway logs are empty and no retry metric exists (F37)
If retries originate at/above the gateway edge, gateway ingress would rise even though retries are the driver — so F25/F41 do not fully exclude H5

ranked_hypotheses.title: Shared redis-cache degradation (possibly triggered by portfolio-service v4.4.0) slowing auth login
ranked_hypotheses.statement: redis-cache is the sole shared component of auth-service's dependency graph (shared:true; consumed by auth-service, portfolio-service, pricing-engine, market-data-service). If redis degraded (a neighbour's load, or a failover), auth login requests hitting the cache would slow/queue, consuming CPU/threads and producing accept-queue saturation. portfolio-service v4.4.0 (dep-5803) is the only deploy in the window and also consumes redis-cache. The critic's blocking point was that redis metrics were never retrieved; those gaps are now filled and F31-F35 affirmatively show redis and all three of its other consumers are healthy and flat — so this hypothesis is now contradicted by direct data, not merely unqueried.

causal_chain.claim: portfolio-service v4.4.0 deploys at 05:50Z — the only deployment in the window, never rolled back
portfolio-service shares redis-cache with auth-service, the only structural path by which a neighbour can degrade auth login

redis-cache shows NO degradation: CPU flat ~22% (min 20.59/max 23.97) with no step at onset; hit ratio flat/healthy ~96% (no miss/cold-cache storm of the HIST-107 kind); connections flat ~310 (no connection storm)

None of the three other redis consumers (portfolio-service, pricing-engine, market-data-service) shows CPU deviation at onset, and portfolio-service p99 is flat ~180ms — the shared path shows no neighbour-side strain
No redis-cache or neighbour deploy/config change exists in or around the window
Therefore a redis degradation would have to route through auth-service as CPU-bound work to produce this signature, which is not supported by any observed redis-side signal

assumptions: redis-cache latency could not be measured directly (no latency_p99_ms metric, F30), so redis slowness is inferred absent from CPU/hit-ratio/clients being flat
A redis degradation would need to route through auth-service as CPU-bound work to produce this signature, which is not the classic cache-slowness profile
ranked_hypotheses.rejection_reason: Direct redis-cache telemetry now contradicts it: CPU flat ~22% with no onset step (F31), hit ratio flat/healthy ~96% with no miss storm (F32), connections flat ~310 (F33); all three other shared-redis consumers show flat CPU (F34) and portfolio-service p99 is flat ~180ms despite being the 05:50Z deployer (F35). The 503 signature is auth-internal ('accept queue full', CPU pinned, autoscaler capped — F9/F10/F29), not downstream cache slowness. The 'not queried' objection that blocked rejection is resolved, so H2 is now excluded by evidence.

ranked_hypotheses.title: Auth-service bcrypt hashing regression reintroduced by an auth-service release (reporter's theory)
ranked_hypotheses.statement: The reporter suspects an auth-service release reintroduced the bcrypt cost regression, making login CPU-bound and producing 503s — matching HIST-101 (bcrypt cost 10->14). The clinical signature matches (login p99 ~4s, 503s, high CPU) but the origin (an auth-service code change) is decisively absent.

causal_chain.claim: An auth-service release raised bcrypt hashing cost, making every login CPU-bound
CPU-bound hashing saturates auth-service, producing accept-queue 503s and ~3.8s p99 — the observed signature
No such release exists: no auth-service deployment in the window (only portfolio-service v4.4.0), and the only auth config change is a non-functional log.level INFO->WARN flip

assumptions: An auth-service deployment in the window was missed by the change queries
ranked_hypotheses.rejection_reason: F1/F14 verified there is no auth-service deployment in the window (the only deploy is portfolio-service v4.4.0); F2/F13 verified the only auth-service config change was a non-functional log.level flag. F6 confirms HIST-101's mechanism required a release. The mechanism signature matches but the origin (an auth-service code change) is decisively absent. The CPU-bound mechanism is real but attributable to a load surge, not a code change (H1).

ranked_hypotheses.title: user-db (postgres) degradation causing login slowness
ranked_hypotheses.statement: auth-service's sole DB dependency is user-db (postgres, shared:false). If user-db degraded (slow queries, connection exhaustion), login requests needing user lookups would block, raising latency and consuming auth-service CPU/threads until the accept queue filled.

causal_chain.claim: user-db is auth-service's only DB edge and is not shared, so only user-db itself degrading can produce login slowness via this path
user-db slowness blocks login DB lookups, backing up auth-service CPU/threads into accept-queue saturation and 503s
The observed surface is inconsistent with blocked DB calls: no timeout or connection-refused errors, memory flat, CPU pinned, worker pool CPU-bound, autoscaler capped

assumptions: No user-db metrics were queried; purely structural
Blocked DB calls would typically produce timeouts/connection errors, which were NOT observed
ranked_hypotheses.rejection_reason: F9 shows no timeout or connection-refused errors — all 503s are 'accept queue full'; F10 shows memory flat with CPU pinned ~97%; F29 shows the worker pool is CPU-bound at 64/64 with the autoscaler capped. Inconsistent with blocked downstream calls.

facts.statement: auth-service p99 latency broke at ~06:53Z: flat ~87-93ms through 06:51Z, then 1969.5ms avg / 3849.2ms max and held ~3.7-3.9s, i.e. before the 07:06Z report.
auth-service error_rate jumped ~70x, from ~0.2% through the 06:50Z bucket to 14.02% at 06:55Z and ~13.6-14.3% thereafter.

All auth-service 503s are 'request rejected: accept queue full, returning 503 (POST /v1/auth/login)' — no timeout or connection-refused errors — with 372 matches from 06:55:42Z to 08:58:57Z and no other endpoint string in any matched ERROR pattern.
auth-service CPU rose from a steady ~36.8-38.6% to 84.31 avg / 97.33 max at 06:50Z and pinned ~96.7-97.7% thereafter, with memory flat (~51-53%), i.e. CPU-bound rather than memory/GC-driven.
auth-service request rate rose ~3.8x at the same onset: ~383-401 req/s through 06:40Z, 1078.03 (max 1813.74) at 06:50Z, and ~1470-1520 req/s from 07:00Z onward.
The worker pool saturated (active=64/64, queue up to 98763) and the autoscaler could not compensate: 'desired replicas 14 exceeds maxReplicas 8; cannot scale further' (first seen 06:57:15Z).
auth-service was not restarted during the incident: cumulative restarts stayed exactly 0.0 at every bucket 06:30-07:30Z.

api-gateway (auth-service's only inbound caller) saw a larger ~3.9-4.1x ingress rise in the identical 06:50-06:58Z ramp, while its error_rate rose only to ~9% and its p99 broke in lockstep with auth-service (~3.95-4.0s), indicating the gateway is blocked waiting on the saturated auth-service rather than failing wholesale itself.

There was no deployment on auth-service (or redis-cache) in the window; the only deployment across all services in 2026-04-20 → 2026-04-22 was portfolio-service v4.4.0 (dep-5803) at 05:50Z, status 'live', never rolled back.

The only config change in the 3-day window was non-functional: auth-service cfg-2801, log.level INFO→WARN at 03:40Z; no auth/bcrypt/JWT/cache parameter was touched, and there was no redis-cache config change.

redis-cache — the only shared component in auth-service's dependency graph (also consumed by portfolio-service, pricing-engine, market-data-service) — showed flat CPU (~22%, min 20.59/max 23.97), flat hit ratio (~96%, no miss storm) and flat connections (~310) across the onset window, and exposes no latency metric at all.

None of redis-cache's three other consumers showed anomaly at onset: portfolio-service, pricing-engine and market-data-service CPU stayed flat (~33-48%), and portfolio-service p99 stayed flat ~180ms (164.7-190.7) despite being the 05:50Z deployer.
user-db is not shared (auth-service is its sole consumer), and the observed surface has no timeout or connection-refused errors, which is inconsistent with blocked downstream DB calls.

Per-caller / per-endpoint / retry breakdown is structurally unobtainable: metrics expose only [cpu_pct, error_rate, latency_p99_ms, memory_pct, rate_limited_per_min, request_rate, restarts] (no request_count_by_caller, no retries_per_min), and logs contain no client IP / user-agent / caller field.

Historical precedent: HIST-101 (2025-08-14) matched this symptom set but was caused by a bcrypt cost 10→14 release and rolled back; HIST-113 shows a capacity_saturation precedent. No such auth-service release exists in the current window.

assumptions: The request-rate increase is genuine exogenous/edge load rather than a retry storm whose retries originate only inside our telemetry; the gateway-ingress evidence (F25/F38/F41) tilts against a single-caller retry origin but does not exclude retries generated at or above the gateway edge.

No autoscaling or limit change explains why maxReplicas is 8; the cap itself was not tested as a recent config change and no evidence places its introduction near onset (it does not change the fix direction).
The surge does not originate in a single shared upstream caller: per-caller breakdown is unavailable (F36/F39), so a caller-concentration origin cannot be measured, only argued against indirectly.

redis latency is judged indirectly from CPU/hit-ratio/connections (F31-F33) because redis-cache exposes no latency metric (F30); a latency-only redis degradation that leaves CPU, hit ratio and clients flat is assumed implausible.
The 63-minute gap between the portfolio-service v4.4.0 deploy (05:50Z) and onset (~06:53Z) is assumed too loose for causality, given portfolio-service's own latency and CPU are flat (F34/F35).

kyc-provider is an external dependency with has_telemetry:false; the assumption that it did not contribute rests only on the absence of timeout/connection errors in auth-service logs (F9), not on direct measurement.

(demoted from facts: no verified observation backs it) auth-service's rate limiter shed inbound traffic from 06:54Z: rate_limited_per_min rose from ~1.65-2.19 req/min to 660.99 (max 919.45) and held ~885-903 req/min — ~15 req/s throttled.

timeline.event: Only in-window config change: auth-service cfg-2801, log.level INFO→WARN (non-functional). 3h13m before onset.
Only deployment across all services in the window: portfolio-service v4.4.0 (dep-5803), status 'live', never rolled back. No auth-service or redis-cache deploy.
Pre-onset baseline: auth-service ~383-418 req/s and p99 ~87-93ms; api-gateway ~1199-1292 req/s; CPU steady ~37-39%; restarts 0.
Onset: auth-service request rate ramps (1078 avg, max 1813.74 req/s), CPU jumps to 84.31 avg / 97.33 max and pins ~97% with memory flat; redis/neighbour CPU and hit ratio remain flat.
auth-service p99 change point: p99 jumps to 1969.5ms avg / 3849.2ms max and holds ~3.7-3.9s.
api-gateway p99 breaks in lockstep to ~3.95-4.0s with error_rate only ~6.96-9.5%; auth-service rate limiting spikes to 660.99/min from ~2/min.
First new auth-service warning: 'worker pool saturated (active=64/64, queue=39035)'.
auth-service error_rate jumps to 14.02% (from ~0.2%) and stays ~13.6-14.3%.
First 'request rejected: accept queue full, returning 503 (POST /v1/auth/login)' error logged.
Autoscaler reports it cannot scale further: 'desired replicas 14 exceeds maxReplicas 8'.
Steady degraded state: auth-service ~1470-1520 req/s at ~97% CPU, p99 ~3.8s, ~14% 503s, restarts still 0.
Incident reported by on-call SRE (reported service auth-service), ~13 minutes after the actual onset.
Last matched 'accept queue full' 503 error in the window; degradation persists to end of data.

recommended_actions.action: Raise auth-service's replica ceiling: change maxReplicas from 8 to at least 14 (the autoscaler's observed desired count) on the auth-service deployment/autoscaling config, then confirm CPU drops below saturation and the accept-queue 503s stop.
recommended_actions.rationale: The autoscaler already computed desired replicas 14 but was blocked at the maxReplicas=8 cap (F29); the ceiling, not the code, is the limiter on a CPU-bound service pinned at ~97% with restarts 0 (F10, F28). This is the only change that directly removes the observed bottleneck.

recommended_actions.action: If the cap cannot be raised immediately, shed or queue excess login load in front of auth-service (tune the existing rate limiter / gateway concurrency) to keep the accept queue from filling, accepting that ~15 req/s are already being throttled.
recommended_actions.rationale: auth-service's rate limiter is already shedding ~885-903 req/min (~15 req/s) and 503s remain, so without added capacity the only stopgap is to bound inbound concurrency rather than let the accept queue fill (F27, F9).

recommended_actions.action: Do NOT roll back or hotfix auth-service code and do not touch config cfg-2801: there is no auth-service deployment or functional config change in the window to revert.
recommended_actions.rationale: Rolling back on the reporter's bcrypt theory (H3) would be an unfounded change; F1/F2/F13/F14 show no auth-service deploy and only a non-functional log.level flag, and F31-F35 affirmatively clear the shared redis-cache/portfolio-service path (H2).

recommended_actions.action: Verify the fix: after capacity is raised, confirm auth-service cpu_pct falls well below ~97%, worker pool active drops below 64/64, accept-queue-full 503s cease, and p99 returns to the ~87-93ms pre-onset baseline; hold for at least the length of the original surge.
recommended_actions.rationale: The onset window is well characterized (F7/F8/F9/F10/F11/F29), giving clear, measurable exit criteria for returning to the pre-onset baseline.

recommended_actions.action: Instrument the missing dimensions needed to close the residual H1-vs-H5 question: add per-caller/per-client-IP and per-endpoint request metrics to auth-service and api-gateway, and a retry/upstream-attempt counter on the gateway, then re-check whether the excess login load comes from many distinct callers or a concentrated retrying caller.
recommended_actions.rationale: Metrics expose only aggregates (no request_count_by_caller, no retries_per_min) and logs carry no client identity (F36/F37/F39), so the origin of the ~3.8x surge — the one untested hop in H1 and the basis for H5 at 0.15 — is currently unmeasurable.

recommended_actions.action: Load-test auth-service at the observed surge level (~1500-1800 req/s, login-heavy) against the new maxReplicas setting to confirm the autoscaler now reaches its desired count and the accept queue never fills; also establish whether login is CPU-bound by hashing cost at this rate.
recommended_actions.rationale: The mechanism chain is fully evidenced (F10/F11/F24/F29) but the capacity headroom needed to serve the observed peak (max 1813.74 req/s, F11/F24) has not been sized; this validates the fix and prevents recurrence at the next surge.

recommended_actions.action: Add redis-cache and neighbour (portfolio-service, pricing-engine, market-data-service) metric series to routine incident dashboards — including a redis latency metric, which does not exist today — so shared-cache hypotheses can be tested in minutes rather than left unqueried.
recommended_actions.rationale: redis-cache exposes no latency metric (F30) and the shared-component path (F4/F15/F19) was only excluded after a round of targeted queries; missing instrumentation delayed excluding H2.

recommended_actions.action: Set replica-capacity guardrails: alarm when sustained CPU exceeds e.g. 80% while the autoscaler reports desired > maxReplicas, and periodically review maxReplicas against observed peak request rates so a provisioned ceiling cannot silently become the bottleneck again.
recommended_actions.rationale: The autoscaler hit the cap at 06:57:15Z yet the incident was only reported at 07:06Z and persisted past 08:58Z (F29, F9); the same class of failure is documented in HIST-113 (capacity_saturation) from F17.

data_gaps: Per-caller / per-client-IP / per-user-agent request breakdown is structurally unavailable for both auth-service and api-gateway, and logs carry no client identity (F36, F39) — this is the single gap capping confidence, since it is the axis that would discriminate H1 (broad exogenous load) from H5 (concentrated retry amplification).

No per-endpoint request/latency metric exists; the 'isolated to POST /v1/auth/login' claim rests on that string being the only endpoint in ERROR logs (F9, F40), not on a positive check that /v1/auth/refresh or /userinfo traffic was normal or elevated.

No retry / upstream-attempt / connection-attempt metric on api-gateway (F37) and no gateway log records at all, so retry volume cannot be measured directly; the anti-retry argument is an inference from gateway ingress rates (F25, F38, F41).

redis-cache has no latency_p99_ms metric (F30), so redis slowness is inferred absent from flat CPU / hit ratio / connections rather than directly measured; redis evictions_per_min and memory_pct were available but not retrieved before the query budget ran out.
auth-service exposes no DB/connection-pool, thread-count or GC metric (F36), so CPU-bound hashing versus downstream DB blocking cannot be fully separated from auth-service's own telemetry.

pricing-engine and market-data-service latency and request_rate for the onset window were not retrieved (budget exhausted), so whether the ~3.8x traffic surge was edge-wide or auth-specific is unconfirmed.
kyc-provider has has_telemetry:false, so any contribution from the external KYC call path is unmeasurable from this dataset.

It was not established whether the maxReplicas=8 cap was introduced recently (no evidence places any autoscaling config change near onset), and it is unclear whether the change backends would surface out-of-scope events (feature flags, infra changes) that could have preceded the surge.
Blast radius outside auth-service/api-gateway remains unverified: no evidence shows whether other services or non-login endpoints degraded in the same window.
what_would_change_the_conclusion: New per-caller or per-client-IP telemetry showing the ~3.8-4.1x surge is dominated by one or a few retrying clients/sources — that would move H5 (retry amplification) above H1 and shift the fix from adding capacity to fixing the retry source.

Direct evidence of a shared-infrastructure fault at onset — e.g. a redis-cache latency spike, failover, hit-ratio collapse or eviction/memory-pressure event, or a degradation step in portfolio-service/pricing-engine/market-data-service — would revive H2 and point at the shared cache or its neighbour rather than auth-service capacity.
Discovery of an unlogged auth-service deployment or a functional auth config/feature-flag change (bcrypt/JWT/cache related) near onset would revive H3 (bcrypt regression) and justify a rollback.

Evidence that the maxReplicas=8 cap was itself changed or mis-configured just before onset (e.g. a recent autoscaling config change) would recast the root cause from demand-driven saturation to a configuration regression, changing the remediation to a config revert.

Evidence that api-gateway itself retries auth-service (gateway-side retry logs or a retry counter showing attempts exceeding inbound requests) would flip the surge from cause to symptom and redirect the fix to the gateway.

A user-db or kyc-provider degradation (slow queries, connection exhaustion, KYC timeouts) appearing at onset would contradict the CPU-bound signature and revive H4 / the external-dependency explanation.

Demonstration that the same surge did not affect any other edge-served service (i.e. traffic is auth-specific) versus an edge-wide surge would refine whether the trigger is global demand or login-specific behaviour.

findings.statement: Across ALL services, the only deployment in 2026-04-20T00:00Z -> 2026-04-22T08:59Z was portfolio-service v4.4.0 (dep-5803) at 2026-04-22T05:50:00Z, author ci-bot, status 'live' and never rolled back. No auth-service deployment exists in the window, so there is no bcrypt-related release to explain the login latency.

The only config change on any service in the same 3-day window was cfg-2801 on auth-service: key 'log.level' changed INFO -> WARN at 2026-04-22T03:40:00Z by config-bot ('Reduce log volume'). No auth/bcrypt/JWT/cache parameter was touched.

auth-service's dependency graph: inbound caller api-gateway --http--> auth-service; auth-service --db--> user-db (postgres, shared=false, only consumer is auth-service); auth-service --cache--> redis-cache; auth-service --external--> kyc-provider (has_telemetry:false).

redis-cache is marked shared:true and is consumed by four services — auth-service, portfolio-service, pricing-engine and market-data-service. This makes it the one component through which a neighbouring service (notably portfolio-service, which deployed v4.4.0 at 05:50Z) could degrade auth-service login without any auth-service change.

user-db is NOT a shared component: its only edge is from auth-service, so auth-service is its sole consumer and a neighbour cannot reach auth-service through it (it can only be the fault if user-db itself degraded).

Historical precedent HST-101 (2025-08-14) is the incident the reporter is referencing: 'Login latency after auth-service release', login p99 4s + 503s + high cpu, root cause 'bcrypt cost factor raised 10->14 in release v6.4.0', category bad_deployment, resolved by rolling back v6.4.0. HIST-107 (2025-12-09) shows a different cause for cache-related latency: 'Cold cache storm after redis failover' on redis-cache/market-data-service, root cause 'Redis primary failure promoted an empty replica', category infrastructure_failure. These are leads only; the current window contains no comparable deployment.

auth-service error_rate change point is between 06:50 and 06:55: it was ~0.2% (0.17-0.31 band all morning) through the 06:50:00Z bucket, then jumped to 14.02% in the 06:55:00Z bucket and stayed ~13.6-14.3% for the rest of the window — a ~70x increase.

The 503 error signature is NOT a timeout or connection-refused: every auth-service ERROR log is 'request rejected: accept queue full, returning 503 (POST /v1/auth/login)' — 59 matches 06:55:42-07:14:54Z in the first query and 372 total matches spanning 06:55:42Z to 08:58:57Z. Only the POST /v1/auth/login endpoint string appears; no other endpoint appears in any matched ERROR pattern.

findings.statement: auth-service CPU saturated at the same onset: cpu_pct was steady ~36.8-38.6% through the 06:40 bucket, then rose to avg 84.31/max 97.33 at 06:50 and pinned at ~96.7-97.7% for the remainder (last 96.97). Memory was flat throughout (~51-53%, min 46.97/max 57.07), so this is CPU-bound, not memory/GC-driven.

Request volume to auth-service ~3.8x'd at the same onset: request_rate was ~383-401 req/s through the 06:40 bucket, then 1078.03 (max 1813.74) at 06:50 and ~1470-1520 req/s from 07:00 onward (last 1504.93). The load surge coincides with the CPU saturation and p99 jump.

The observed symptom is server accept-queue saturation (CPU-bound): all three signals — cpu_pct ~97%, error_rate ~14%, p99 ~3.8s — flip in the 06:50-06:55 window, ~10-16 min earlier than the 07:06Z report, and auth-service reported only POST /v1/auth/login errors while CPU was pinned at ~97%, which is consistent with hashing cost under a load surge rather than a downstream dependency error (no timeout/connection-refused messages appear).

refs.quote: request rejected: accept queue full, returning 503 (POST /v1/auth/login)

findings.statement: The only change on auth-service in the incident window (or the 3 days before it) is a non-functional logging flag: cfg-2801, key 'log.level' INFO->WARN at 2026-04-22T03:40:00Z by config-bot ('Reduce log volume'), 3h13m before the ~06:53Z onset. No auth/bcrypt/JWT/cache parameter was touched, so there is no config change temporally or causally aligned with the degradation.

No deployment exists on auth-service (or redis-cache) in the incident window: the only deployment across all services is portfolio-service v4.4.0 at 2026-04-22T05:50:00Z (dep-5803, 'Holdings export', status 'live', never rolled back), and scoping to redis-cache returns count 0. This removes the bcrypt-regression/bad-deployment mechanism for the current incident.

redis-cache is the single shared component in auth-service's dependency graph (shared:true, consumed by auth-service, portfolio-service, pricing-engine and market-data-service) and is the only structural path by which the 05:50Z portfolio-service release could degrade auth-service; user-db is not shared. However, redis-cache has no recorded deployment or config change of its own in the window, so a redis-side change is not recorded.

portfolio-service (the sole deployer in the window, 05:50Z) also consumes redis-cache and calls market-data-service and ledger-db; its release added a 'CSV export endpoint' and no portfolio-service config change exists in 2026-04-20->2026-04-22, so its change footprint is limited to the v4.4.0 code deploy.

Temporal alignment: the portfolio-service deployment (05:50Z) precedes the auth-service onset (~06:53Z) by 63 minutes, whereas the prior bcrypt-regression precedent HIST-101 has symptoms 'login p99 4s', '503 on login', 'high cpu' but is categorized bad_deployment and was caused by a release (bcrypt cost factor 10->14, rolled back) -- no such release exists here. A capacity-saturation precedent does exist (HIST-113: pricing-engine, 'quote timeouts', 'cpu 99%', root cause 'Record market-open volume exceeded provisioned capacity', category capacity_saturation).

findings.statement: The three candidate explanations sort on timing and signature: (a) bcrypt regression is contradicted (no auth-service deploy/config; F1/F2), (b) downstream-dependency slowness is unsupported by the observed surface (T1: 503s are 'accept queue full' with memory flat, not timeouts or connection-refused) and no redis-cache/user-db change is recorded, (c) resource saturation best fits the data already reported -- CPU 38%->97% under ~3.8x request rate (390->1500 req/s) with server accept-queue rejects on POST /v1/auth/login. The unverified link is what produced the request-rate surge.

redis-cache is shared:true and is the sole shared component of the four consumers — auth-service, portfolio-service, pricing-engine, market-data-service each have a 'cache' edge into redis-cache; no other datastore links these four.

No deployment on redis-cache in 06:30-07:30Z (count 0), and none across all services in 06:00-08:00Z (count 0): the only deployment in the wider incident window remains portfolio-service v4.4.0 at 05:50Z.
No config change on redis-cache in 06:30-07:30Z (count 0), and none across all services in 06:00-08:00Z (count 0); the only config change in the 3-day window remains auth-service cfg-2801 at 03:40Z.

redis-cache has no downstream dependents (downstream query returns empty edges), confirming it is a leaf datastore whose behaviour can only be observed via its own metrics, not via its own call graph.

Historical precedents for a shared-cache fault (HIST-107, 2025-12-09, redis-cache + market-data-service, symptoms 'cache miss storm' / 'quote latency', root cause 'Redis primary failure promoted an empty replica', category infrastructure_failure) and for capacity saturation (HIST-113, 2026-01-28, pricing-engine, 'quote timeouts'/'cpu 99%', 'Record market-open volume exceeded provisioned capacity') both exist, but neither reports an auth-service login symptom — so they are leads only and neither matches the current symptom set exactly.

auth-service request_rate rose from a flat pre-onset baseline (~382-413 req/s through the 06:48Z bucket) to 671.71 (max 770.48) at 06:51:00Z, 1154.93 at 06:54:00Z, peak 1641.69 (max 1813.74) at 06:57:00Z, then held ~1412-1546 req/s through 07:30 — roughly a 3.8x sustained increase, matching F11.

api-gateway (auth-service's only inbound caller) shows a LARGER and proportionally heavier surge than auth-service in the same window: request_rate was ~1239-1277 req/s through the 06:48 bucket, then 2102.78 (max 2490.76) at 06:51:00Z, 3530.13 at 06:54:00Z, 4486.2 at 06:57:00Z, and ~4685-5247 req/s from 07:00 onward (last 5247.87) — a ~4.1x rise vs auth-service's ~3.8x. Because the gateway's own ingress rate grows at least as much as what it forwards, the surge originates at/above the gateway's edge rather than being a single caller's retries against auth-service.

findings.statement: api-gateway's error_rate rose only modestly and its latency broke in lockstep with auth: error_rate was ~0.15-0.26% through the 06:50 bucket, then 6.96% (max 9.4) at 06:54:00Z and ~8.8-9.5% thereafter; latency_p99_ms was flat ~206-219ms through 06:50, then jumped to 3952.31ms (max 4200.87) at 06:54:00Z and held ~3.8-4.0s. The gateway itself is not failing wholesale (~9% 5xx) but its tail latency tracks auth-service's ~3.8s p99, i.e. the gateway is blocked waiting on the saturated auth-service.

findings.statement: auth-service rate limiting spiked exactly at the onset: rate_limited_per_min was ~1.65-2.19 req/min through the 06:50 bucket, then 660.99 (max 919.45) at 06:54:00Z and ~885-903 req/min for the rest of the window (last 885.3) — a ~400x jump, i.e. roughly 900 req/min (15 req/s) of the inflowing traffic was throttled rather than served.

findings.statement: auth-service was NOT restarted anywhere in 06:30-07:30Z: the cumulative restarts metric is exactly 0.0 at every bucket (min 0.0, max 0.0, first 0.0, last 0.0). The degradation is not a crash/restart loop; it is a live process pinned at a capacity ceiling.

Endpoint/caller breakdown from auth-service logs: the only error/rejection endpoint is POST /v1/auth/login — top pattern 'request rejected: accept queue full, returning <n> (POST /v<n>/auth/login)' count 104, first_seen 06:55:42Z. The first new warning appears at 06:54:53Z 'worker pool saturated (active=64/64, queue=39035)' and the pool stays pinned at 'active=64/64' with queues up to 98763, and the autoscaler cannot help: 'autoscaler: desired replicas 14 exceeds maxReplicas 8; cannot scale further' (first_seen 06:57:15Z). No /v1/auth/refresh or other endpoint appears in any matched log pattern.

findings.statement: redis-cache exposes NO latency metric: a query for latency_p99_ms on redis-cache failed with not_found and listed the only available metrics as connected_clients, cpu_pct, evictions_per_min, hit_ratio_pct, memory_pct. So redis latency must be judged indirectly (hit ratio, clients, CPU, evictions).
redis-cache CPU is FLAT across the 06:40-07:10Z onset window: min 20.59 / max 23.97 / mean 22.07, with 21.38-22.5% at 06:50-07:00 and no step at the ~06:50-06:53Z onset. No redis-side CPU stress.

redis-cache hit ratio is FLAT and healthy across the window: min 94.44 / max 97.32 / mean 96.09%, 96.8% at 06:50, 96.09% at 06:54, 96.21% at 07:08 — no miss storm, no cold-cache signature of the HIST-107 kind.

redis-cache connection count is FLAT across the window (min 285.87 / max 336.83 / mean 310.54 clients; 309.09 at 06:50, 308.58 at 06:54, 318.48 at 07:06). No connection-pool growth or connection storm at onset — the only rising quantity on the auth path is auth-service's own CPU, not redis connections.

None of the three redis-cache-sharing neighbours shows CPU deviation at the ~06:50-06:53Z onset: portfolio-service cpu_pct stayed ~32.86-39.44 (mean 35.93; 34.31 at 06:50, 37.08 at 06:54), pricing-engine ~38.8-43.6 (mean 39.95; 40.34 at 06:50, 39.53 at 06:54), market-data-service ~41.39-48.17 (mean 45.38; 46.73 at 06:50, 45.38 at 06:54). All three are flat and well below the ~97% that auth-service reached.

portfolio-service latency_p99_ms is flat across the onset: min 164.72 / max 190.67 / mean 180.04ms (186.86 at 06:50, 180.84 at 06:54, 166.25 last) — no degradation despite being the 05:50Z deployer. Its p99 is ~20x lower than auth-service's ~3.8s, so portfolio-service is not sharing the auth symptom.

The metrics API exposes NO per-caller/source and NO per-endpoint dimension for either service: api-gateway's available_metrics are exactly [cpu_pct, error_rate, latency_p99_ms, memory_pct, request_rate, restarts], and a request for a caller dimension fails: "service 'api-gateway' has no metric 'request_count_by_caller'". auth-service's available_metrics are [cpu_pct, error_rate, latency_p99_ms, memory_pct, rate_limited_per_min, request_rate, restarts]. So breakdown by client IP / user-agent / caller is impossible; the most granular obtainable is the total per-service request_rate.

No retry-related gateway metric is exposed: request for retries_per_min on api-gateway fails with "service 'api-gateway' has no metric 'retries_per_min'", and its full available_metrics list contains no retry, upstream-attempt, connection-attempt or queue metric. Retries cannot be quantified from gateway metrics.

Aggregate per-service request_rate for the 06:30-07:10 window (only granularity available): auth-service baseline is flat ~383-418 req/s through 06:48, then ramps 452 (06:50), 743 (06:52), 1095 (06:54), 1350 (06:56), peak 1750 avg / 1813.74 max (06:58), settling ~1442-1534 req/s 07:00-07:10 (last 1469.29) — ~3.8x. api-gateway over the same window: flat ~1199-1292 req/s through 06:48, then 1501 (06:50), 2328 (06:52), 3294 (06:54), 3940 (06:56), 4790 (06:58), ~4661-4991 req/s 07:00-07:10 (last 4990.58) — ~3.9x. Both rims ramp over the same 06:50-06:58 interval with no step unique to one side.

auth-service logs contain NO client-identifying dimension (no client IP, user-agent, caller, or API-key field) — every entry is a bare message such as a queue/pool line or endpoint string, so caller concentration cannot be derived from logs either. The 06:45-07:10 slice returns 84 matches: 44 ERROR, 36 WARN, only 4 INFO, and every ERROR is the same endpoint string.

Endpoint dimension from logs shows only ONE endpoint ever appears: across auth-service log patterns the only error endpoint is POST /v1/auth/login (count 44 in this slice, first_seen 06:55:42Z), with no /v1/auth/refresh, /userinfo or any other endpoint string in any matched pattern. This is consistent with load/retries concentrated on login, but it is equally explainable by login being the CPU-expensive endpoint under a broad surge — it cannot distinguish H1 from H5.

Directional evidence against a pure client-retry loop: the gateway's OWN ingress request_rate rises ~3.9x in the identical 06:50-06:58 ramp (1199-1292 -> peak 4859.74 max, last 4990.58), i.e. load is elevated at/above the gateway's ingress, not only on gateway->auth-service retries; and auth-service's own rate limiter had to shed ~885-903 req/min (~15 req/s) of inbound traffic from 06:54 on. Retries could still be generated at/above the gateway edge, so this narrows but does not eliminate H5.
